questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bending in a stone lintel
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stress state that makes a stone lintel crack
questions.stem: A mason sets a single stone lintel across a 3 m opening in a rubble wall and finds it cracked along its underside after two winters. Which account of the failure fits best?

options.text: The lintel bent as a simply supported beam, so the underside of its middle was in tension and cracked
The lintel failed because the wall load exceeded the stone's crushing strength along the top of the beam
options.misconception: assumes stone fails in compression before tension

options.text: The lintel failed because the mortar joints could not transfer the wall's weight sideways into the jambs
options.misconception: blames the bed joints instead of bending

options.text: The lintel failed because the wall above settled unevenly and cracked the stone in pure shear
options.misconception: reads a tension crack as a shear failure

questions.explanation: A lintel spans an opening as a simply supported beam, with tension at the underside and compression at the top. Stone is weak in tension, so cracking at midspan underside is the expected signature.
questions.hint: Ask which face of a bending beam is in tension.

questions.topic: Why an arch outlives a lintel
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the horizontal thrust of a parabolic arch from span and rise
questions.stem: A design brief for a 10 m clear opening specifies a parabolic arch of rise 2.5 m carrying a uniform load of 8 kN per metre along the span. Using the relation H = wL^2/(8f), what horizontal thrust in kN must the springings resist?
questions.explanation: For a parabolic arch under uniform load the horizontal thrust is wL^2/(8f). With w = 8 kN/m, L = 10 m and f = 2.5 m this gives 800/20 = 40 kN. A beam of that span shows no horizontal component.
questions.hint: Use H = wL^2/(8f) with the rise in metres.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The keystone in the ring
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a ring without its central stone loses stability

stimulus.body: A restoration survey at a partly collapsed chapel records that a semicircular arch over the crossing had been rebuilt twice, each time with the central wedge-shaped stone missing. Flanking arches whose central stones survive show no measurable distortion. A junior engineer wonders whether the crossing arch was always unstable.

questions.stem: Given the survey record, which explanation for the repeated failure of the crossing arch best fits the pattern?

options.text: The missing wedge let rainwater into the bed joints, weakening the arch whatever its structural state
options.misconception: blames water ingress instead of the compression line

options.text: Without its central wedge the ring cannot lock into one continuous compression line, so the voussoirs spread
The rebuilds used softer limestone, so the arches failed from poor material rather than faulty geometry
options.misconception: blames material quality instead of the ring geometry

options.text: The crossing arch carried more load than the flanking arches, so the missing wedge only confirms an overload
options.misconception: assumes greater load rather than a missing closing stone

questions.explanation: The central wedge locks the ring into one continuous compression line; without it the voussoirs splay as separate cantilevers. Flanking arches that kept their central stones show the geometry and loading were sound.
questions.hint: Ask what holds the compression line together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the blocks are wedges
questions.learningObjective: Explain why voussoirs are cut as wedges
questions.stem: Two masons argue about why the voussoirs for a new arch are cut as wedges rather than as plain rectangular blocks, and ask which reason the survey team should record.

options.text: Wedge shapes make the ring watertight by squeezing mortar into the joints as the arch settles
options.misconception: treats the wedge shape as a waterproofing device

options.text: Wedge shapes lighten the ring so that the springings no longer need deep foundations beneath them
options.misconception: believes taper reduces weight rather than transmitting thrust

options.text: Wedge shapes let each block press on its neighbour along angled faces instead of relying on friction alone
Wedge shapes let the arch be dismantled and rebuilt if the loads later prove to be wrong
options.misconception: sees the wedge only as a convenience for dismantling

questions.explanation: Each voussoir passes thrust to the next along a face square to the thrust line, so the ring works in compression. The angled faces carry the load; friction and self-weight only resist sliding.
questions.hint: Think about how a wedge pushes, not pulls.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pier under a vault must resist
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a vault pier resists vertical load and lateral thrust together
questions.stem: In a structural brief for a crossing pier, explain why a pier that carries a masonry vault has to resist both a downward load and an outward horizontal push.

answer.exemplar: The vault bears down on the pier with the weight of the masonry above it, and it also pushes outward at the springing because the thrust of the ring has to go somewhere. A pier sized only for the vertical share offers nothing to react that sideways push, so the ring spreads and the vault cracks along its springing.

questions.explanation: The vault delivers its masonry weight plus an outward horizontal component at the springing. A pier sized only for gravity cannot react that push, so the ring spreads and the vault cracks.
questions.hint: Trace where the arch's thrust goes.

questions.stem: A monitoring sheet from a 13th-century hall lists four bays. The end bays have solid end walls; the two middle bays have arcade walls with tall windows between the piers. Which structural reading fits the sheet?

options.text: The piers in the middle bays are decorative, and the real support comes from the thickness of the end walls
options.misconception: dismisses the piers and credits the end walls

options.text: Vault loads run continuously along the wall head in every bay, so the windows are decorative additions
options.misconception: reads the wall head as a continuous load path

options.text: Only the end bays are vaulted, and the middle bays are roofed in timber that the windows ventilate
options.misconception: assumes timber roofing instead of a vault

options.text: Arcade bays send vault loads to discrete piers, so the infill wall carries little and can be opened for windows

questions.explanation: Ribs gather the vault load into the piers at bay corners, so the wall between them is infill that can be opened for windows. A continuous wall-head load path would wrongly demand a solid wall.
questions.hint: Ask where the ribs deliver their load.

questions.stem: A cathedral survey team is asked two things: first, why the choir walls can carry very large windows, and second, which element actually delivers the vault's sideways push into the ground.

options.text: The wall thickens toward the ground and absorbs the vault thrust internally, with no outer support needed
options.misconception: assumes a thick wall can react the thrust alone

options.text: The flying buttress carries the vault thrust out to a separate outer pier, leaving the choir wall as light infill
Iron in the window tracery is stiffened to work as a strut between the vault and the buttress
options.misconception: credits the window ironwork with a thrust path

options.text: The choir is vaulted in timber rather than stone, so the vault produces no horizontal thrust to carry
options.misconception: assumes a timber vault creates no thrust

questions.learningObjective: Relate the rise of an arch to the thrust it delivers
questions.stem: Two masons argue about why a tall round arch in good repair still stands while a flatter arch of the same stone has failed nearby. Which account of the difference is correct?

options.text: The taller arch stands because it was built later and benefited from better stone-cutting techniques
options.misconception: credits later workmanship rather than geometry

options.text: The flatter arch failed because its voussoirs were laid with too much mortar and so behaved as soft blocks
options.misconception: attributes the failure to mortar instead of thrust

options.text: The taller arch pushes less horizontally because its rise is larger, so it makes less demand on its supports
The flatter arch failed because it had a keystone while the taller arch was built without one
options.misconception: reverses the role of the central wedge

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The keystone in the ring
questions.learningObjective: Describe how the central voussoir closes an arch ring

stimulus.body: A restoration survey at a Romanesque abbey records three semicircular windows. The largest arch has its central voussoir set slightly proud of the ring with no mortar in its upper joint, while the two smaller arches have their central stones bedded flush and fully mortar-jointed. The mason asks what the report should say about how the ring is held together.

questions.stem: Which statement should the survey report include about how an arch ring is held together and closed?

options.text: The ring is held by the weight of the masonry above, so the central stone carries the greatest share
options.misconception: believes the crown block takes the greatest load

options.text: The ring is held by the mortar in its bed joints, and the central voussoir is purely decorative
options.misconception: credits mortar with closing the ring

options.text: The ring is held by iron cramps let into the extrados, with the central stone added to cover the joint
options.misconception: credits cramps rather than the closing stone

options.text: The central voussoir closes the ring by wedging the two halves of the arch against one another

questions.explanation: The central voussoir is placed last; driving it wedges the two halves of the ring together so the whole works in compression. Mortar and cramps hold individual pieces but do not close the ring.
questions.hint: Think about the order in which stones are placed.

questions.topic: Why the blocks are wedges
questions.learningObjective: Select the voussoir shape that suits the thrust in a ring
questions.stem: A worksheet lists four voussoir sets for one arch: set A has parallel sides, set B tapers upward at 30 degrees, set C tapers upward at 45 degrees, and set D widens upward. Which set belongs in the ring?

options.text: Set A, because parallel-sided blocks bed most evenly on the mortar and are easiest to dress
options.misconception: prioritises easy bedding over thrust transfer

options.text: Set B or set C, because each block must present faces roughly square to the thrust it passes along
Set D, because widening faces open the ring so the central stone can be driven more easily
options.misconception: thinks a wider ring aids the closing stone

options.text: Set B alone, because a 45 degree taper leaves joint faces unable to carry any thrust at all
options.misconception: treats a steeper taper as structurally useless

questions.explanation: A voussoir works best when its joint faces are roughly square to the thrust it transmits, so the block presses instead of sliding. Tapered sets of 30 or 45 degrees do that; parallel beds rely on mortar.
questions.hint: Ask which way the joint faces point.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pier under a vault must resist
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the base and shaft of a pier under a vault
questions.stem: In a note to the parish architect, explain why a pier carrying a vault needs a broad base as well as a heavy shaft, and what would happen if it did not have one.

answer.exemplar: The vault delivers a large vertical load plus a horizontal thrust that arrives at the springing as a slanting resultant. The shaft must carry that resultant down as compression, so it is built thick and massive. The base widens the bearing area so the load is spread over the ground without exceeding the soil's bearing capacity, and it resists the overturning moment that the horizontal component creates.

questions.explanation: The vault's resultant arrives at the springing as a slanting force, so the pier must be massive enough to carry it as compression. The base spreads it over enough ground to stay within the soil's bearing capacity.
questions.hint: Think about the resultant at the springing.

questions.topic: The load path of a ribbed vault
questions.learningObjective: Trace the load path from ribbed vault to foundation
questions.stem: Two questions are asked of the vault engineer: which part of a ribbed vault carries the load, and where that load is finally delivered.

options.text: The bosses at the intersections carry the load outward to the clerestory walls along the nave
options.misconception: treats the carved boss as a structural carrier

options.text: The webbing between the ribs carries the load to the wall head, which is thick enough to take it
options.misconception: credits the webbing with the main load path

options.text: The ribs carry the load to the bay corners, where piers on the ground take it down to the foundations
The vault carries its own weight along the ridge line to the ends of the church and no further
options.misconception: assumes the load runs along the ridge only

questions.explanation: A ribbed vault concentrates load into ribs that run to the bay corners, which sit over piers carrying the resultant to the foundations. The webbing spans between ribs rather than the wall.
questions.hint: Follow the ribs down to the ground.

options.misconception: attributes a crack to earlier warping

options.text: The lintel shows a chalky white bloom on its top surface, suggesting that the stone is porous
options.misconception: reads a weathering bloom as structural distress

options.text: The mortar joints on the upper face have washed out, leaving small gaps where water collects
options.misconception: treats washed-out joints as a bending sign

options.misconception: believes the deeper curve mainly adds vertical load

options.text: A deeper curve reduces horizontal thrust, so the existing springings will be asked to carry less sideways load
A deeper curve removes the need for a central wedge, because the ring can close without it
options.misconception: thinks depth of curve removes the keystone

options.misconception: confuses curve depth with voussoir taper

questions.topic: Why the blocks are wedges
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an arch drops when its central stone is removed

stimulus.body: A conservation note describes how a medieval arch was dismantled for repair. The mason recorded the order of removal: the blocks were taken out one at a time from the side of the arch toward the crown, leaving the central stone in place until the very last step. When the central stone was finally eased out, the remaining half of the arch dropped and broke.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the mason's experience of the arch dropping when the central stone came out?

options.text: Removing the central stone removed the only weight holding the arch down, so the whole ring lifted
options.misconception: imagines the ring lifting when the block came out

options.text: Removing the central stone released the horizontal thrust stored in the ring, which then pushed the arch sideways
options.misconception: credits the release of thrust rather than lost support

options.text: Removing the central stone broke the compression line, so the remaining voussoirs lost their mutual support
Removing the central stone let water into the open joint and weakened the mortar in the ring
options.misconception: blames water for a mechanical collapse

questions.explanation: A closed ring supports itself through mutual compression, which is why it stands while the central stone is in place. Removing that block leaves two cantilevers that cannot stand, so the arch drops.
questions.hint: Think about what the closed ring does for itself.

options.misconception: blames spandrel weight rather than lateral thrust

options.text: The compressive strength of the pier's core, since the arch has been pressing down on it for centuries
options.misconception: reads a horizontal crack as a crushing failure

options.text: The tensile strength of the pier's face stones, which crack horizontally under downward loading

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a ribbed vault
questions.learningObjective: Explain why vault webbing can be thinner than its ribs
questions.stem: In a maintenance log, explain why the webs between the ribs of a vaulted ceiling can be built much thinner than the ribs themselves.

answer.exemplar: The ribs are the members that gather the load of the vault and carry it down to the piers, so they are built deep enough to span between the supports without bending. The webbing between them only has to close the space between two ribs that are already supported at their ends. It therefore behaves like a shallow arch or a slab spanning a short distance, and can be made much thinner.

questions.explanation: The ribs span between supports and gather the load, so they need depth to avoid bending. The webbing only closes the gap between two already supported ribs, so it spans a short distance and can be thin.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece spans between.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the quarry batch that supplies voussoirs

stimulus.body: A quarry delivery note for a church repair lists four batches of dressed stone. Batch one consists of long rectangular blocks for walling. Batch two consists of wedge-shaped blocks with tapered beds, ordered at two different taper angles. Batch three is a single long dressed bar intended to span a doorway. Batch four is a stepped block intended to sit at the foot of a column.

questions.stem: Which batch supplies the voussoirs for the arch, and what feature of those blocks makes them work?

options.text: Batch one, because long rectangular blocks bed evenly and so spread the thrust through their joint faces
options.misconception: believes rectangular blocks transmit thrust well

options.text: Batch two, because tapered beds present faces roughly square to the thrust, letting the ring act in compression
Batch three, because a long dressed bar is the standard way to close an arch ring
options.misconception: confuses a lintel with an arch ring

options.text: Batch four, because a stepped block at the foot of a column is what locks the ring together
options.misconception: attributes ring closure to a column base

questions.explanation: Tapered beds give each voussoir faces roughly square to the thrust it passes along, so blocks press on one another and the ring works in compression. Rectangular blocks rely on mortar instead.
questions.hint: Look at the shape of the bed joints.

questions.learningObjective: Compare thrust per unit load across a set of arches
questions.stem: A table of arch spans lists four openings with their rises: 4 m span with 1.3 m rise, 6 m span with 2 m rise, 8 m span with 2.7 m rise, and 10 m span with 3 m rise. Which opening produces the greatest horizontal thrust per unit of load?

options.misconception: believes rise does not affect the thrust

options.text: The 4 m span with a 1.3 m rise, because a shallow rise always multiplies the horizontal thrust
options.misconception: assumes the smallest arch always thrusts hardest

options.text: The 10 m span with a 3 m rise, because its span to rise ratio is the least steep of the four

answer.exemplar: A pier is a vertical support that carries weight downwards from a vault or an arcade, standing as a column of masonry beneath the point where the load is delivered. A buttress is a mass of masonry built against or beside a wall to resist the sideways thrust that the vault or arch throws out of it. The pier takes the load down; the buttress takes the push sideways. In practice a single masonry mass can do both jobs at once, which is why the terms get used interchangeably.

questions.hint: Compare the direction of each load.

answer.exemplar: A lintel behaves as a beam, and its bending stress depends on the moment it carries divided by its resistance, which for a rectangular section grows with the square of the depth. Doubling the span quadruples the moment, while a depth of one twelfth of the span keeps the stress roughly constant. The practical rule is therefore that a wider opening needs a proportionally deeper stone, since stone tolerates very little tension at its soffit.

questions.explanation: The bending moment grows with the square of the span, while the section resisting it grows with the square of the depth. Doubling the span therefore needs a deeper stone to keep soffit tension tolerable.

questions.explanation: The band area is half the difference of two circles: 1.5708 x (12.96 - 9) = 6.22 square metres. Times the 0.8 m length of the ring this gives about 4.976 cubic metres of stone.
questions.hint: Treat the ring as half of a hollow circle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pier under a vault must resist
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the base and capital of a vault pier
questions.stem: A structural engineer notes that a pier under a vault has a wider base than its shaft and a moulded top. Which reading of those two features is correct?

options.text: The wide base is purely a matter of appearance, and the moulded top is a decorative transition
options.misconception: dismisses both features as decoration

options.text: The wide base resists the vault's outward thrust, and the moulded top resists the ground's upward pressure
options.misconception: swaps the jobs of base and capital

options.text: The wide base spreads the load over the ground, and the moulded top spreads the vault's load down the pier
The wide base lets more weight bear on the soil, and the moulded top reduces the pier's own weight
options.misconception: treats the base as increasing soil pressure

questions.explanation: A wider base enlarges the bearing area so the load from the pier stays within the soil's capacity, and the moulded capital spreads the concentrated thrust of the vault over the full width of the shaft.
questions.hint: Consider soil bearing and load spread.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The load path of a ribbed vault
questions.learningObjective: Explain uneven rib deflection from measured readings

stimulus.body: An instrument log from a vault records the deflection of each of the four ribs in a bay over one year. Two ribs adjacent to the piers show a slow downward movement of 6 mm and 7 mm, while the two ribs on the far side show 1 mm and 2 mm. The readings are taken at the crown of each rib, and the webs between them show no cracking. The engineer notes that the pier on the high side was repointed two years ago.

questions.stem: Which reading of the instrument log best explains the uneven rib deflections?

options.text: The webs are stiff enough to hold the ribs level, so the readings must come from the instruments
options.misconception: dismisses the readings as instrument error

options.text: The ribs have stretched in the heat of two summers, and the webs are insulated against that movement
options.misconception: blames seasonal thermal movement for the readings

options.text: One rib was built with poorer stone, and the log simply records the difference in material quality
options.misconception: attributes the readings to stone quality

options.text: The two piers have settled by different amounts, so the ribs span to different levels across the bay

questions.explanation: Ribs span between piers and take the shape their supports allow, so a rib on a settled pier hangs lower. The difference between adjacent ribs matches the settlement, and the webs are sound.
questions.hint: Ask what the ends of the ribs are standing on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the wall can be opened up
questions.learningObjective: Compare a braced and an unbraced church wall
questions.stem: A comparison of two arches in the same church shows one with a wall thickness of 2.2 m and no external buttress, and the other with a 0.6 m wall braced by a flyer. What does the pair show?

options.text: The braced arch has a thinner wall because the builder chose economy over structural soundness
options.misconception: reads the thinner wall as mere economy

options.text: The braced arch can be built with a thinner wall because its thrust is led out to an outer pier
The unbraced arch has a thick wall because thick walls were the standard fashion of the period
options.misconception: explains the thick wall as a style choice

options.text: The two arches are unrelated, and the wall thickness simply reflects the size of the opening
options.misconception: treats the two examples as independent

questions.explanation: Unbraced churches need thick walls to resist the vault's outward thrust. Where the thrust is led to an outer pier the wall can be thin: a structural difference, not a stylistic one.
questions.hint: Compare the thickness with the bracing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Bending in a stone lintel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why lintels are more sensitive to support movement than arches
questions.stem: In a short essay brief, explain why a stone lintel is more vulnerable to movement of its supports than an arch of similar span and material.

answer.exemplar: A lintel is a single rigid beam whose ends are simply supported, so any settlement or rotation at one jamb makes the whole beam tilt and crack along its underside. An arch is a ring of small blocks that can redistribute its forces around the curve when a support moves slightly, so a small settlement opens a joint or two rather than breaking the member. The arch therefore tolerates movement of its supports far better than the lintel, which is why it is used where the foundations are uneven.

questions.explanation: A lintel is one rigid beam that tilts and cracks at the soffit if a jamb settles. An arch is a ring of blocks that redistributes forces round the curve, opening a joint rather than breaking.
questions.hint: Compare a single member with a ring.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an arch outlives a lintel
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a keystone-less arch stands and what it costs
questions.stem: Two tasks are given to the mason: name the feature that lets an arch stay stable without a central wedge, and say what it costs the arch.

options.text: The weight of the masonry in the spandrels, which steadies the arch at no cost to its stiffness
options.misconception: claims the spandrel weight costs the arch nothing

options.text: The wedge shape of the voussoirs, which makes the arch carry load twice as well as a closed ring
options.misconception: credits the taper with the stability

options.text: The hinge at the crown and the springings, which makes it a three-hinged arch of lower stiffness
The thickness of the jamb walls, which stabilise the arch without changing how it deflects
options.misconception: claims thick jambs cost no extra deflection

questions.explanation: An arch with hinges at the crown and each springing is a three-hinged arch, stable on its own. The price is that hinges permit movement, so it deflects more and reacts badly to settlement.
questions.hint: Count the hinges in the arch.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The keystone in the ring
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the horizontal thrust of a wide arch
questions.stem: A thrust estimate for a 16 m span arch of 4 m rise carries a uniform load of 15 kN per metre along its span. Using H = wL^2/(8f), what horizontal thrust in kN is delivered at each springing?
questions.explanation: With w = 15 kN/m, L = 16 m and f = 4 m the thrust is 15 x 256 / (8 x 4) = 120 kN. Each springing also carries half the total load, so the vertical share is also 120 kN.
questions.hint: Substitute into H = wL^2/(8f).

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the blocks are wedges
questions.learningObjective: Identify the masonry evidence of a corbelled rather than true arch
questions.stem: A survey team concludes that the arch over a side doorway was never a true arch but a corbelled arrangement of flat stones. What feature of the masonry would confirm that reading?

options.text: The stones of the ring are all wedge shaped with a constant taper from one side to the other
options.misconception: mistakes true voussoirs for a corbelled ring

options.text: Every stone in the ring is a rectangular block with parallel bed joints, as in ordinary walling
options.misconception: treats parallel beds as evidence for a true arch

options.text: A single large stone spans the whole opening at the crown, with rubble packed around it
options.misconception: reads a single spanning stone as a corbelled ring

options.text: Each successive stone projects a little further inward, so the ring is stepped rather than rotated

questions.explanation: A corbelled arch is built by stepping flat stones so each projects beyond the one below, giving a polygonal opening rather than a curve. A true arch uses rotated voussoirs whose beds follow the curve.
questions.hint: Look at how the opening is shaped.
